label: Motion Descriptions and Diagrams
description: Connect dot spacing, velocity changes, and acceleration direction; compare each interval before deciding how an object moves.
commonMisconception: Students treat equal spacing as 'constant speed' even when direction changes, or infer acceleration direction from velocity direction rather than from the change in spacing between successive dots.

label: Interpreting Kinematics Graphs
description: Distinguish what the graph's axes represent; connect slope to the derived quantity and height to the state quantity; for direction changes require sign comparison across the zero crossing.
commonMisconception: Students conflate slope and value on v-t and x-t graphs (e.g., reading a v-t graph's height as position, or claiming 'changing direction' whenever the v-t curve crosses zero without checking sign before and after).

label: Vectors, Signs, and Units
description: Separate magnitude-units from direction requirements; verify that a negative sign encodes direction relative to a chosen positive axis, not a 'smaller' quantity.
commonMisconception: Students treat units alone as sufficient to classify a quantity (e.g., 'm/s downward' is a velocity but '9.8 m/s² downward' is not), or ignore that a signed scalar component (e.g., −120 m/s) is a valid velocity representation.

label: Kinematics Calculations
description: Require time-weighted averaging for multi-leg trips; force explicit listing of knowns before equation selection; check that the chosen equation contains the target variable and only knowns.
commonMisconception: Students average speeds arithmetically over unequal-time legs, or reach for Δx = ½at² without accounting for nonzero initial velocity; sign errors also appear when direction reverses.

label: Force Diagrams and Net Force
description: Require every force to be identified by an external object; net force direction must come from vector sum, not from velocity; constant velocity means zero net force regardless of speed.
commonMisconception: Students draw forces in the direction of motion, add a separate 'force of motion,' or believe constant velocity requires a net force in the direction of travel.

label: Newton's Third Law Pairs
description: Apply the two-object test: each pair member acts on a different object, same interaction, equal magnitude, opposite direction; mass and acceleration do not modify pair magnitudes.
commonMisconception: Students select a same-object partner force (e.g., normal force as the pair to gravity on a table) or reason that the larger/faster object exerts more force; pairs must act on different objects with equal magnitude regardless of motion outcome.

label: Qualitative Newton's Second Law
description: Separate acceleration (from net force) from velocity (from prior state); zero net force preserves whatever velocity exists; a shrinking net force shrinks acceleration, not speed.
commonMisconception: Students believe zero net force means the object stops (rather than continues at constant velocity), or that a decreasing net force means decreasing speed rather than decreasing acceleration; direction of acceleration is conflated with direction of velocity.

label: Newton's Second Law Calculations
description: Require a defined system before writing ΣF = ma; distinguish mass (inertia, kg) from weight (gravitational force, N); for two-body systems identify which object's forces belong in the equation.
commonMisconception: Students divide force by acceleration incorrectly (or invert), assume gravitational force changes when the same block moves to the Moon (mass vs. weight confusion), or apply F=ma to a multi-object system while ignoring internal forces.

label: Vector Components and Normal Force
description: Choose useful axes, resolve vectors into components, and connect the perpendicular component of weight to the normal force on a surface.
commonMisconception: Students set the normal force equal to mg on every surface, swap the sin and cos assignments for the parallel and perpendicular components, or believe the normal force is a fixed reaction to weight independent of surface orientation.

label: 2-D Equilibrium and Connected Systems
description: Force component decomposition along chosen axes before summing; tension transmits the interaction but each body gets its own ΣF = ma; connected systems share one acceleration magnitude.
commonMisconception: Students sum force magnitudes directly without components (e.g., treating 60 N + 75 N as the missing force), assume tension is the same in non-ideal rope segments with different geometry, or ignore that connected bodies share acceleration but not force.
